etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English particuler, from Anglo-Norman particuler, Middle French particuler, particulier, from Late Latin particularis (“partial; separate, individual”), from Latin particula (“(small) part”). Equivalent to particle +‎ -ar. Compare particle.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) Pertaining only to a part of something; partial.

quote.citation: c. 1599–1602 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Hamlet, Prince of Denmarke”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene v]:
quote.text: I could a tale unfold whose lightest word / Would harrow up thy soul, freeze thy young blood, / Make thy two eyes, like stars, start from their spheres, / Thy knotted and combined locks to part / And each particular hair to stand on end

definitions.definition: Specialised; characteristic of a specific person or thing.

quote.citation: 1625, Francis [Bacon], “Of Gardens”, in The Essayes […], 3rd edition, London:  […]  Iohn Haviland for Hanna Barret, →OCLC:
quote.text: wheresoever one plant draweth such a particular juice out of the earth

definitions.definition: (obsolete) Known only to an individual person or group; confidential.

quote.citation: c. 1603–1606, William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of King Lear”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene i]:
quote.text: or these domesticke and particular broiles, Are not the question heere.

definitions.definition: Distinguished in some way; special (often in negative constructions).
(comparable) Of a person, concerned with, or attentive to, details; fastidious.

quote.citation: 1929, Sir Arthur Conan Doyle, When the World Screamed‎[1]:
quote.text: There is a scraper as well as a mat, and Mrs. Challenger is most particular.

definitions.definition: Concerned with, or attentive to, details; minute; circumstantial; precise.

quote.citation: 1765–1769, William Blackstone, Commentaries on the Laws of England, (please specify |book=I to IV), Oxford, Oxfordshire:  […]  Clarendon Press, →OCLC:

definitions.definition: (logic) Forming a part of a genus; relatively limited in extension; affirmed or denied of a part of a subject.
A small individual part of something larger; a detail, a point. [from 15th c.]

quote.citation: 1726 October 28, [Jonathan Swift], “Several Contrivances of the Author to Please the King and Queen. […]”, in Travels into Several Remote Nations of the World.  […]  [Gulliver’s Travels], volume I, London:  […]  Benj[amin] Motte, […], →OCLC, part II (A Voyage to Brobdingnag), page 259:
quote.text: I did not omit even our Sports and Paſtimes, or any other Particular which I thought might redound to the Honour of my Country.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) A person's own individual case. [16th–19th c.]

quote.citation: 1603, Michel de Montaigne, chapter 16, in John Florio, transl., The Essayes […], book II, London:  […]  Val[entine] Simmes for Edward Blount […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Since philosophy could never find any way for tranquillity that might be generally good, let every man in his particular seeke for it.

quote.citation: 1658, Henry Hammond, Whole Duty of Man:
quote.text: temporal blessings, whether such as concern the public […] or such as concern our particular

definitions.definition: (now philosophy, chiefly in plural) A particular case; an individual thing as opposed to a whole class. (Opposed to generals, universals.) [from 17th c.]

quote.citation: 1912, Bertrand Russel, The Problems of Philosophy, Chapter 9:
quote.text: When we examine common words, we find that, broadly speaking, proper names stand for particulars, while other substantives, adjectives, prepositions, and verbs stand for universals.
